newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-DON POOLE LEADS ATLANTA CLASSIC AFTER FIRST ROUND.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-DON POOLE LEADS ATLANTA CLASSIC AFTER FIRST ROUND.

text.p: American Don Pooley continued his resurgence when he earned a two-stroke lead after the opening round at the $1.5 million BellSouth Atlanta Classic Thursday.

"It's probably been 10 years since I've hit the ball this well," said Pooley, who missed only one fairway and one green as he compiled eight birdies in a moderate afternoon breeze for a flawless eight-under-par 64, a course record on the newly-opened Sugarloaf TPC.
Fellow Americans Donnie Hammond, Scott Simpson, Bobby Wadkins and David Duval, and Zimbabwe's Nick Price were equal second on 66.
Course designer Greg Norman, the world number one, made a dream start with an eagle at his first hole, but had a nightmare finish with bogeys at his final two holes for a 70.
Pooley, 45, has won twice on the PGA Tour, most recently at the 1987 Memorial, but he lost his card last year after finishing 169th on the money list.
However, as a past champion on tour, he qualified for a one-year, one-time exemption, which he decided to take up this year.
It has proved a wise decision to date, because he is a healthy 45th on the money list after making the cut in all eight events he has contested.
"I had a lot of (birdie) chances and made a bunch of them," Pooley said. "I've always been a good putter and I'm putting well this year again, but my ball hitting last year was terrible.
"I got a lesson in January from Jim Flick, made a couple of changes in my swing, and I'm hitting the ball like I did back in 1987. It's been a long time."
Pooley was full of praise for the course. "I think Greg did a great job. It reminds me of an old-style course, a strategic course, where you have options to play different shots."

Price, meanwhile, continued his hot form in his first competitive round since he won the MCI Heritage Classic three weeks ago -- and he had finally obtained a club that he likes from the company he endorses commercially.
"The new driver's in the bag and I'm very happy," said Price, who carried his clubs in a Goldwin bag at Harbour Town, even though he was not playing any of the company's clubs.
He is even more buoyed by the news that his long-time caddie, Jeff "Squeeky" Medlen, apparently is doing well in his battle against leukaemia.
"He's really excited. He's turned the corner. There's a good chance he may have kicked the whole thing," Price said of Medlen, who is battling the disease in a Columbus, Ohio, hospital.
"I couldn't have wished for anything better right now. I spoke to his wife on Tuesday and then I spoke to "Squeek" and just by the tone in their voices, you can feel the happiness."
